methodological_questions: How to define closest pre-absence initiation profile (cosine, initiations, minutes, same-position)?
How to define primary play types of the absent player?
How to measure the largest gainer in those types (absolute increase, proportion of vacant share)?
How to control for confounding by lineup changes, opponent quality, game script, and other absences?
Is the number of absence episodes sufficient to power a meaningful test?

historical_evidence.finding: Mean replacement similarity ABSORBED +0.863 vs CASCADE +0.848; Spearman(sim, -gap) = -0.19 (wrong-signed). Embiid 23-24 cascades with Reed sim 0.94. Similarity does not separate absorption from cascade; almost always findable.
Team offensive association structure persists across split halves (Frobenius S=0.352 p<0.01), and this persistence is not reducible to play-type rates (residual R²=0.043).
Connector absence displaces team offensive identity (D_A) more than usage-matched non-organizer absence, t=5.97 p=2.87e-08, n=96 matched pairs.
Real absence moves association structure (C1 pass), but the leave-one-out simulation failed to predict the magnitude (Spearman rho=0.288 p=0.077).
Named star initiators (Jokic, Curry, Doncic, Giannis) have identifiable lineup and forced-play-type suppressors, but no placebo or matching was applied.
78 players with BEST vs AVOID head-to-head PPP gaps, some large (Lively II +1.833), but small per-player sample (min 5 rows/tier) and no multiplicity correction.
Pooled player-level BEST vs AVOID gap +0.427 PPP, but only 3 players clear n≥30 in both tiers (all Boston Celtics).
Usage-residual influence is reproducible: F1a residual share 0.906, cosine R²=0.094; F1b pooled-residual rank correlation rho=0.685.
On/off identity displacement larger for shapers (ΔD_A=+0.115, t=6.35, p~7e-9), and leave-one-out loss L(p) correlates with observed D_A (r=0.60 overall, shapers +0.79).
Connector presence does not shield stars (TS p=0.937, TO p=0.00364 wrong sign). Lineup ORtg lift is a talent confound (p=0.51 after control).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using play-type similarity to predict absorption vs cascade
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null result: similarity does not separate outcomes; Spearman(sim, -gap) = -0.19; Embiid cascaded with high-similarity teammate. RISK: LABEL_ERROR also noted.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Connector tangible impact on star shielding and lineup ORtg lift
failed_approaches.why: Adequately powered null: PPP/TS/eFG shielding null; TO rate rises with connectors; lineup lift disappears after talent control. RISK: CONFOUNDING, SMALL_SAMPLE.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Player-level BEST vs AVOID PPP gap exploration
failed_approaches.why: Question not answerable (A_unanswerable): tiny per-player samples (min 5 rows), no multiplicity control, classification dependent on single-game playsheets.
Untestable: simulation prediction correlation not significant (p=0.077), small sample (23 absences), failure to confirm validation step V2.

evidence_establishes: Similarity-based prediction of absorption vs cascade is not supported; even high similarity coexists with cascade outcomes (FAM:SF-CHT-052).
Team offensive identity is persistent and responds to connector/shaper absences in a way not reducible to usage (SF-APPS-088, SF-PAP-014).
Play-type statistics at the player level suffer from small per-cell counts and low reliability when gates are applied (SF-APPS-036, SF-APPA-048).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a specific metric of 'closest pre-absence initiation profile' (e.g., cosine similarity, minutes, initiations, same-position) can identify the teammate who gains most in the absent player's primary play types.
The prior study used a binary absorption/cascade outcome, not continuous gain measurement. The current question's gain metric may behave differently.
The historical null does not rule out a weak effect that would remain undetectable with the extremely limited number of absence episodes.
own_inferences: The extremely low number of independent absence cases (n=11) and total spells (148) is the strongest limiting factor; within-team comparisons of gainers will be underpowered even if a large effect existed.
Confounding by game context, opponent strength, simultaneous absences, and coaching decisions makes causal attribution of 'largest gainer' to similarity alone very difficult.
The prior null result on similarity indicates low prior probability of a positive finding; combining that with the small sample makes a conclusive test unlikely.
uncertainties: Exact operational definitions of 'closest pre-absence initiation profile', 'largest gainer', and 'primary types' are not specified in the question.
The data catalog (play-by-play, substitution, matchup minutes) may allow calculation of pre-absence profiles, but the reliability of play-type classification (the 'primary types') is not reported.
No power calculation has been performed; the effective degrees of freedom (absence-level clustering, multiple teammates) are unknown.
Whether additional seasons or pooling could increase the effective sample to a useful level is not addressed in the current data request.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history, the question might appear novel and worth exploratory analysis. The retrieved record FAM:SF-CHT-052 directly tested a very similar hypothesis—similarity predicting teammate absorption vs cascade—and obtained a null result with indicated adequate power. That negative precedent, combined with the tiny sample (11 cases), shifts the default judgment from 'exploratory proceed' to 'do not proceed' because the chance of a robust positive test is minimal.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 11 cases and 148 spells; multiple teammates per absence event reduce independent units; power to detect a non-trivial effect is very low.
The specific play-type possessions an absent player would have taken are sparse; computing gain for each teammate in those exact types often yields zero or single-digit possessions per game.

prior_work.summary: SF-CHT-052 addressed 'Play-type replacement similarity vs absorb/cascade' and concluded that similarity does not separate absorption from cascade, with a powered null. The present question is a variant (largest gainer in primary types), but the underlying mechanism—similarity predicting which teammate fills the void—was effectively tested and found null.

risks.text: 11 absence cases and 148 spells severely limit power for any player-level comparison; cross-validation or permutation tests would have very low resolution.
Many absence episodes involve stars with high usage, but the 'primary types' may represent a small fraction of total possessions; teammate gain in those types is noisy.
Play-type classification (the 'primary types') relies on automated tagging from play-by-play, which can misclassify similar actions; errors propagate to both profile and gain metrics.
Lineup composition changes, opponent defensive strategy, game score, and simultaneous other absences all influence who gets those possessions, confounding the similarity–gain relationship.
Selection of absence episodes based on sufficient on-off sample may bias toward games with large swing; regression to the mean in teammate gain could produce spurious associations.
Comparing multiple teammates within each absence (all candidates for 'closest' and 'gainer') inflates false positive risk unless multiplicity adjustment is used.
Initiation profile stability for players with limited minutes or many play-type categories is low; cosine similarity may be unreliable for players with short pre-absence periods.
If the absent player's primary types overlap heavily with the team's overall offense, all teammates may gain, making the 'largest gainer' distinction trivial.

design.estimand: For each absence episode, the difference in possession share (or points per possession) in the absent player's primary play types between the teammate with the closest pre-absence initiation profile (cosine similarity or highest minutes/initiations) and the average of all other teammates, controlling for lineup and opponent.
design.unit: An absence spell (contiguous games a player misses) with at least 200 possessions on-court for the team before the spell and at least 100 possessions during the absence.
design.sample: All absence spells meeting gates across 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons, stratified by position and usage tier; projected n ≈ 30+ spells after gates (currently only 11 cases in the stated data, so expansion to additional seasons or playoff data would be needed).
design.power: Given prior null (FAM:SF-CHT-052), a moderate effect (d=0.5) would require ~35 independent spells to achieve 80% power at alpha=0.05 one-tailed; the current 11 cases yield power <30%.
design.controls: Lineup composition (five-player fixed effects or clustered standard errors), opponent defensive rating, game location, rest advantage, and simultaneous other absences via regression adjustment.
design.falsification: (1) Placebo test: randomly permuting the absent player's type profile across episodes should nullify the similarity-gain correlation. (2) Non-absence control: within the same team, randomly selected games with full roster should show no systematic gainer for the most similar teammate.
design.multiplicity: Bonferroni correction for the number of primary play types (up to 5) and for testing multiple similarity definitions (cosine, minutes, initiations, same-position).
design.decision_rule: Proceed only if after pooling available spells, power simulation with bootstrapped residuals yields ≥80% power for a Cohen's d ≥ 0.3. Pre-registered primary metric is Spearman rank correlation between similarity rank and gain rank among teammates.
design.data_version: Play-by-play and derived play-type records from NBA stats API for seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26, as of 2026-10-31 freeze, with play types defined by the Neo4j graph taxonomy used in prior studies.

methodological_questions: How to define closest pre-absence initiation profile?
How to measure primary play types of the absent player?
How to quantify the largest gainer in those types?
How to control for confounding by lineup changes, opponent, and game context?
What sample size is needed for reliable inference on individual teammate gains?
